column2: This is e, raised to the power of a matrix. A grid of four numbers, sitting where an exponent should be. What could that possibly equal?
It equals this. A rotation of the whole plane, by exactly one radian. That's about fifty-seven degrees. By the end, you'll see why it couldn't be anything else.
First, what is a matrix? A grid of numbers that works as a rule. Feed it an arrow, and it hands back a new arrow.
This particular grid turns every arrow a quarter turn. We'll call it J, and it comes back later.
E squared is e times e. But e, multiplied by itself a matrix number of times? That means nothing.
So try the obvious repair. Raise e to each entry, one at a time.
Test the guess on the easiest matrix of all, four zeros. E to the zero is one, so the guess gives four ones. Is that right?
No. E to the zero should change nothing. And the matrix that changes nothing has ones on its diagonal, and zeros everywhere else.
Four ones do something violent. They squash the whole plane onto a single line.
So the guess is dead. To find the real meaning, we have to ask what e to the x has meant all along.
Start with money. One dollar, in a bank that pays a hundred percent a year. After one year, two dollars.
Now split the year in two. Fifty percent, twice. The second step earns on the first, so you end with two twenty-five.
Your turn, and pause the video whenever you want longer. Four steps give two forty-four. Twelve give two sixty-one. Keep cutting the year finer. Does the total grow without limit?
No. It settles. A step every day gives two point seven one five. A million steps give two point seven one eight two eight. That number is called e.
Every step followed one rule. Grow by a share of what you have. Shrink the steps to nothing, and the rule becomes this. Your rate of growth equals your size.
That's the first face of e to the x. The one curve whose steepness, everywhere, equals its height.
Here's a second way to reach that curve. Build it piece by piece, so that its rate equals itself.
Start with one. Its rate is zero, and we need one. So add x, which climbs at a rate of one.
Now x needs a partner whose rate is x. That's half of x squared, the area under the line. An area grows as fast as its leading edge is tall.
To match that one, add x cubed over six. Every new piece supplies the rate of the piece before it. So what comes after x cubed over six?
X to the fourth, over twenty-four. Each bottom number is the one before, times the next whole number. One, two, six, twenty-four. The factorials.
Carry on for ever, and the sum is its own rate. Each piece turns into the piece before it, so the whole row slides one place over, and nothing is lost.
Try it at x equals one. One, plus one, plus a half, plus a sixth. The running total climbs to two point seven one eight. The same number the bank gave us.
That's no coincidence. The tiny steps and the series obey the same rule, rate equals size, from the same start. Only one curve can.
And this is why e to the x simplifies so much. Whenever a rate is proportional to an amount, the answer is e, to the rate times the time.
Savings, bacteria, radioactive decay, a cooling cup of coffee. One function handles them all.
Your turn. Something grows at five percent a year, continuously, for twenty years. How many times bigger does it get?
Five percent times twenty is one. So it grows by e to the one. Two point seven one eight times.
Last, grow for a while, then a while longer, and the factors multiply. E to the a plus b equals e to the a, times e to the b. Remember that rule. It's going to break.
Now feed that function something strange. The number i. Forget square roots for a moment. Multiplying by i means one thing. Turn a quarter turn.
So make your rate i times your position. That's a push sideways. Always at right angles to where you stand.
Follow that rule in tiny steps, each one a small push sideways. What path do you trace?
A circle. Four big steps drift outward. A hundred hug the circle. In the limit you stay on it exactly, and after a time t, you have turned through an angle t.
Run it for a time pi, half a turn, and you land on minus one. E to the i pi equals minus one. Growth, pushed sideways, is rotation.
Back to the matrix. Look at what the series asks of x. Multiply it by itself. Divide by whole numbers. Add.
A square matrix can do all three. So put a matrix where the x was. That is the definition of e to a matrix.
Your turn. Try it on J, the quarter turn. The series needs J times J, which means, do a quarter turn, twice. What is J squared?
A half turn. Every arrow reversed. That's minus the matrix that changes nothing. So J behaves exactly like i.
So the series sorts itself into two piles. The even powers are plain numbers. The odd powers are numbers times J.
Those two piles are the cosine and the sine. So e to the t J is the rotation by the angle t. And at t equals one, it's the matrix from the very start.
But an endless sum of matrices? What would it mean for that to have an answer? That the running total settles, in every entry. Mathematicians say the series converges.
Here's a worrying case. E to five times J. Its terms get big. Two of them have entries near twenty-six.
Your turn. Each new term multiplies by five again, and divides by the next whole number. What happens to the terms from here?
They collapse. Once you're dividing by six, seven, eight, the factorial wins. By the twentieth term, about forty millionths. And the running total spirals home, to a point on the circle.
And that works for every square matrix. Measure a matrix by its size, the most it can stretch any arrow. Multiply two matrices, and their sizes at most multiply.
So the k-th term is never bigger than the size to the k, over k factorial. Those numbers add up to e to the size, which is finite. The matrix series sits underneath, so it settles. Every time.
So e to a matrix exists. But what does it mean? Go back to tiny steps.
Read the matrix as a rule for motion. Wherever you are, apply the matrix to your position, and that's your velocity. Where you're headed, right now.
Now follow the arrows for a time t. Every point lands somewhere new. The matrix that carries each start to its finish is e to the t A.
Follow them for a time s. Then for a time t more. What single matrix does the whole trip?
E to the s plus t, times A. Run, and run again, is one longer run. The rule of exponents, kept.
The matrix is the rule for tiny steps. Its exponential is the result.
A real one. Two tanks, a hundred litres each, with pumps swapping ten litres a minute. Stir a hundred grams of salt into the left tank.
Every minute, a tenth of each tank's salt crosses over. Two equations, one for each tank. Together they are one matrix.
Where is the salt after ten minutes? Take it as one big step, and the rule says all hundred grams change tanks. Absurd.
Ten steps say about fifty-five grams stay. A thousand steps say fifty-six point seven five. E to the ten A gives the answer in one stroke. Fifty-six point seven seven.
Your turn. Leave the pumps running for hours. Where does the salt end up?
Fifty grams in each. And the exponential says how fast. Within a gram of even, after about twenty minutes.
A matrix can also be a map. Four nodes, some of them linked. Write a one where two nodes are linked, and a zero where they aren't.
Multiply that matrix by itself, and each entry counts something. The number of two-step walks between a pair of nodes.
Your turn. Start at node three. How many two-step walks bring you back to node three?
Three. Out along any of its three links, and straight back. The matrix agrees.

The k-th power counts walks of k steps. So e to this matrix adds up every walk of every length, and divides a walk of k steps by k factorial. Long walks count for less. Infinitely many walks, one function.
Network scientists call that number communicability. How well two nodes are connected, counting every route between them, and not only the shortest.
Now let something flow along the links. Put heat on node four. Each link carries heat from its hotter end to its cooler end.
That rule is a matrix too, so the answer is its exponential. Watch the heat spread, and level out. A quarter on each node.
Your turn. Same network, new meaning. A hopper jumps along the links at random. After a long time, which node is it most likely to be on?
None of them. A quarter each. The busy node in the middle gets more visitors, and loses them just as fast.
And the two tanks were this all along. Two nodes, one link, settling at half and half.
Now put the letter i into the exponent. The same two nodes never settle. The chance sloshes across, and back, for ever. That is how quantum physics moves in time.
So how does a computer find e to a matrix? Surely it adds up the series.
Try this matrix, from a famous paper. Nineteen Dubious Ways to Compute the Exponential of a Matrix.
Its terms swell past nine million, with alternating signs. They have to cancel down to four numbers smaller than two.
A computer that keeps about seven digits adds up that series, until the total stops changing. How good is its answer?
Wrong in every entry. One even has the wrong sign. The mathematics is fine. The digits that mattered were thrown away long before the end.
The cure is the oldest idea in this video. Tiny steps. Halve the matrix eight times, so its series is short and tame. Then square the result, eight times.
Real libraries do exactly that, with a sharper stand-in for the short series. A ratio of two polynomials, called a Padé approximant.
And when a matrix untangles into separate rates, you exponentiate each rate alone. That's the eigenvalue story, which has a video of its own.
Remember the rule we said would break? E to the a plus b equals e to the a, times e to the b.
Your turn. Swap the numbers for two matrices, A and B. Does the rule still hold?
Take two shears. A pushes the top of a square to the right. B pushes its right side upward.
Follow A, then B. Now B, then A. Now both rules at once. Three different shapes.
The rule broke because order matters. A then B is not B then A. When the order makes no difference, we say two matrices commute, and for those, the rule holds.
And the failure can be measured. Take one order away from the other. A B, minus B A. That leftover is called the commutator, and it is the first correction to the broken rule.
That leftover is a doorway. Go back to rotations. The quarter turn J has a special shape. Flip it across its diagonal, and every sign changes.
Every matrix of that shape exponentiates to a rotation, and every rotation comes from one. In three dimensions there are three basic ones. A spin about each axis.
Your turn. Three dimensions, three independent spins. How many are there in four dimensions?
Six. A spin doesn't really happen around an axis. It happens in a plane, and four axes make six pairs.

And spins don't commute. Tip a little about x, a little about y, then undo each one. You are not back where you began. What's left over is a small spin about z. The commutator of two spins is a third spin.
The spins, with that commutator, form a Lie algebra. The rotations they generate form a Lie group. And the exponential is the bridge from one to the other.
Lie groups are the mathematics of smooth motion. A robot arm's pose is a product of exponentials, one for every joint. That's the companion video, on Lie groups and robotics.
And in particle physics, the forces of the Standard Model are built on three Lie groups. Their independent tiny steps number eight, three, and one. Twelve in all. What might those twelve be?
The particles that carry the forces. Eight gluons. The W plus, the W minus, and the Z. And the photon.
So that's what it means to raise e to a matrix. The matrix is a rule for tiny steps. E to the matrix is where that rule takes you.
Growth, turning, heat, chance, rotation. One function, following one rule. Its rate is itself.
